To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the errors in stored grain inventory determination are dominated by errors in the measurement of the grain height, and that errors in the measurement are not independent of the grain height.
the error in determining the inventory in a bin is a function of the number of bins, the number of samples, and the number of samples per bin.
The inventory determination error for the entire grain mass is the sum of errors for individual bins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
determining the error in the inventory of stored grain that is determined using a non-destructive method.
the development and validation of a methodology for determining the mass of stored grain in a grain storage facility.
developing and evaluating a method to estimate the inventory of stored grain in a bin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the error associated with the determination of stored grain inventory is a function of the number of grain samples taken, the number of grain subsamples taken, the number and size of the grain test samples, and the number of test samples analyzed.

the errors associated with inventory determinations using a single point sampling technique are not as high as previously thought and that a 5% error in the inventory estimate can be achieved with a sample size of 50 to 75 samples.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that a new approach to determining grain inventory is feasible.
there are many sources of error in stored grain inventories and the errors can be significant in terms of both magnitude and variability.
the error in the stored grain inventory determination was less than 2% of the actual inventory for the three methods used to estimate the inventory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a variety of sources of error in stored grain inventory determinations.
